examples.en: This city developed with a distorted structure.

examples.ko: 기형적인 가격 때문에 아무도 그 물건을 안 사요.
examples.en: Nobody buys that item because of its abnormal price.
House prices have risen abnormally lately.
That building has a rather misshapen form.

examples.ko: 이런 기형적인 관계는 오래 못 가요.
examples.en: A lopsided relationship like this can't last long.

examples.ko: 우리나라 인구 구조가 기형적이라는 말을 자주 들어요.
examples.en: I often hear that our country's population structure is distorted.

explain: '이상하다'보다 정상에서 크게 벗어났다는 비판의 느낌이 강해요. 가격, 구조, 성장, 관계처럼 추상적인 것에 주로 쓰고, 사람의 몸에는 쓰지 않는 게 좋아요. '기형적인 구조', '기형적으로 오르다'처럼 뒤에 명사나 동사가 와요.
explain_en: It carries a stronger critical feel than '이상하다' (strange), meaning something has strayed far from normal. It is mostly used for abstract things like prices, structures, growth and relationships, and it is best not to use it for people's bodies. It is followed by a noun or verb, as in '기형적인 구조' or '기형적으로 오르다'.

examples.ko: 모든 학생에게 교육 기회균등이 보장돼야 해요.
examples.en: Equal opportunity in education must be guaranteed for every student.

examples.ko: 이 회사는 채용에서 기회균등을 가장 중요하게 생각해요.
examples.en: This company considers equal opportunity the most important thing in hiring.
Equal opportunity is easy to talk about but hard to put into practice.

examples.ko: 기회균등의 원칙을 지키지 않으면 불만이 생겨요.
examples.en: If the principle of equal opportunity isn't kept, complaints arise.

examples.ko: 기회균등 없이는 공정한 사회가 될 수 없어요.
examples.en: Without equal opportunity, a society can't be fair.

examples.ko: 오늘 수업에서 기회균등에 관한 토론을 했어요.
examples.en: In class today we had a discussion about equal opportunity.

explain: 뉴스, 토론, 교육·채용 이야기에서 자주 나오는 말이에요. 결과를 똑같이 만든다는 뜻보다 출발선에서 같은 기회를 준다는 쪽에 가까워요. '기회균등을 보장하다', '기회균등을 실현하다'처럼 같이 써요.
explain_en: It often appears in news, debates, and talk about education and hiring. It leans toward giving everyone the same chance at the starting line rather than making the results equal. It pairs with verbs like '보장하다' (guarantee) and '실현하다' (realize).

examples.ko: 그 사람은 이기는 쪽만 따라가는 기회주의자예요.
examples.en: He's an opportunist who only follows the winning side.
His friends called him an opportunist.
An opportunist changes what he says when the situation changes.
I don't want to look like an opportunist.

examples.ko: 회의에서 그는 기회주의자 같은 태도를 보였어요.
examples.en: At the meeting he showed an opportunistic attitude.
Don't entrust important work to an opportunist.

explain: 자기에게 유리한 쪽으로 입장을 바꾸는 사람을 비판할 때 써요. 상대 앞에서 말하면 꽤 심한 모욕이 되니 조심해요. 비슷한 '눈치가 빠르다'는 나쁜 느낌이 거의 없어서 느낌이 달라요.
explain_en: It is used to criticize someone who changes sides to benefit themselves. Saying it to someone's face is a fairly harsh insult, so be careful. The similar '눈치가 빠르다' (quick to read the room) has almost no negative feel, so the nuance is different.

examples.en: An opportunistic attitude makes you lose trust.
That politician changed his position opportunistically.
If my behavior was opportunistic, I apologize.
Opportunistic people don't have many friends.
He was criticized for being too opportunistic.
Even if it's an opportunistic choice, I can understand it.

explain: 사람의 태도나 행동, 선택을 평가할 때 쓰고 거의 항상 부정적이에요. '기회주의적인 태도', '기회주의적으로 행동하다'처럼 써요. 사람 자체를 말할 때는 '기회주의자'를 써요.
explain_en: It is used to judge someone's attitude, actions or choices, and it is almost always negative. Use it as in '기회주의적인 태도' or '기회주의적으로 행동하다'. When talking about the person himself, use '기회주의자'.

examples.en: Korea belongs to the temperate climate zone.
The plants that grow differ depending on the climate zone.

examples.ko: 열대 기후대에서는 일 년 내내 더워요.
examples.en: In a tropical climate zone it's hot all year round.
Try dividing the climate zones by color on the map.

examples.ko: 이 지역은 두 기후대가 만나는 곳이에요.
examples.en: This region is where two climate zones meet.
When the climate zone changes, people's way of life changes too.

explain: 지리 수업이나 설명문에서 많이 나와요. '열대, 온대, 냉대, 한대' 같은 말과 같이 써요. 일상 대화에서는 '이 지역 날씨는 어때요?'처럼 말하는 편이에요.
explain_en: It appears a lot in geography classes and explanatory texts, together with words like 열대 (tropical), 온대 (temperate), 냉대 (cool-temperate) and 한대 (polar). In everyday talk people would just ask about the weather of a region instead.

examples.en: I wasn't sure whether the rumor was true.

examples.ko: 그 사람이 그 배우가 맞는지 긴가민가 하면서 쳐다봤어요.
examples.en: I looked at him, unsure whether he was that actor.
I wrote the answer without being sure, and it was right.

examples.ko: 처음엔 긴가민가 했는데 이제 확실히 알겠어요.
examples.en: At first I wasn't sure, but now I know for certain.

examples.ko: 길이 맞는지 긴가민가 해서 지도를 다시 봤어요.
examples.en: I wasn't sure it was the right way, so I looked at the map again.
I kept wondering whether it was true, and in the end I called.

explain: 맞는지 아닌지 확실하지 않을 때 쓰는 구어체 말이에요. 보통 '~인지 긴가민가'처럼 의문을 나타내는 말과 같이 나와요. 형용사 '긴가민가하다'로도 쓰니 같이 알아 두세요.
explain_en: It is a colloquial word for when you can't tell whether something is so or not. It usually follows a clause with '~인지' (whether). It also works as the adjective '긴가민가하다', so learn them together.

examples.en: I'm not sure this is the right way.
I'm still not sure whether that story is true.
I wasn't sure, so I asked once more.
I can't tell if the answer is number 3 or 4.

examples.ko: 그 사람을 아는 것 같기도 하고 아닌 것 같기도 해서 긴가민가했어요.
examples.en: I felt I might know him, or might not, so I wasn't sure.
If you're not sure, check first.

explain: 확실하지 않아서 판단이 안 설 때 쓰는 말로, 말할 때 많이 써요. 비슷한 '헷갈리다'는 둘 이상이 섞여 구별이 안 될 때, '긴가민가하다'는 맞는지 아닌지 모를 때 써요. '맞는지', '사실인지' 같은 말과 자주 같이 나와요.
explain_en: It is a spoken-style word for when you can't decide because you aren't certain. '헷갈리다' is for when things get mixed up and you can't tell them apart, while '긴가민가하다' is for not knowing whether something is true or not. It often follows clauses like '맞는지' or '사실인지'.

examples.ko: 긴말할 필요 없이 결과로 보여 드릴게요.
examples.en: No need to say much; I'll show you with results.
I don't have time today, so I won't go on at length.
He didn't say much and just nodded.
Talking at length won't change anything.
I don't want to drag it out, so I'll start with the conclusion.

examples.ko: 긴말하면 오히려 변명처럼 들릴 것 같아요.
examples.en: If I go on at length, it might sound like an excuse.

explain: 대부분 '긴말하지 않다', '긴말할 필요 없다'처럼 부정이나 거절하는 말투로 나와요. 명사 '긴말'을 써서 '긴말 안 할게요', '긴말 필요 없어요'라고도 해요. 결론만 말하겠다고 할 때 자연스러워요.
explain_en: It mostly appears in negative or dismissive forms like '긴말하지 않다' or '긴말할 필요 없다'. People also use the noun '긴말', as in '긴말 안 할게요'. It is natural when you say you'll just give the conclusion.

examples.en: The two countries are cooperating closely.
The team members work while keeping in close contact.

examples.ko: 이 문제는 관계 기관과 긴밀히 상의해야 해요.
examples.en: We need to consult closely with the related agencies on this issue.
I'm contacting you because I have something to discuss in confidence.
The police are working in close coordination with the school.
If departments communicate closely, mistakes decrease.

explain: 협력하다, 연락하다, 소통하다, 상의하다처럼 서로 주고받는 동작과 같이 써요. '가깝게'보다 격식 있어서 업무, 뉴스, 공식적인 말에서 많이 나와요. 형용사 '긴밀하다'는 '긴밀한 관계'처럼 써요.
explain_en: It goes with verbs of exchange such as 협력하다 (cooperate), 연락하다 (contact), 소통하다 (communicate) and 상의하다 (consult). It is more formal than '가깝게' and is common in work, news and official talk. The adjective '긴밀하다' is used as in '긴밀한 관계'.

examples.ko: 이 영화는 처음부터 끝까지 긴박감이 넘쳐요.
examples.en: This movie is full of tension from beginning to end.
I could feel the urgency in the breaking news.

examples.ko: 음악 때문에 장면의 긴박감이 더 커졌어요.
examples.en: The music made the sense of urgency in the scene even stronger.
The novel had no suspense, so it was a bit boring.

examples.ko: 구조 현장의 긴박감은 말로 다 설명할 수 없어요.
examples.en: The urgency at the rescue site can't be fully put into words.

examples.ko: 그 소식을 들은 순간 긴박감에 숨이 막혔어요.
examples.en: The moment I heard the news, the urgency took my breath away.

explain: 사건이 급하고 아슬아슬하게 돌아갈 때 느끼는 분위기를 말해요. 영화, 소설, 뉴스, 구조 현장 이야기에서 '긴박감이 넘치다', '긴박감을 주다'처럼 자주 써요. 단순히 바쁜 것은 '바쁘다'라고 해요.
explain_en: It describes the tense mood when events are urgent and on a knife edge. It is often used for movies, novels, news and rescue scenes, as in '긴박감이 넘치다' or '긴박감을 주다'. Simply being busy is just '바쁘다'.

examples.en: The government announced an austerity policy this year.
The company got into trouble, so it switched to a tight budget.
Because of the belt-tightening, salaries didn't go up.
Our household is in austerity mode these days too.
When the economy gets worse, every country goes into austerity.
If austerity drags on, people's spending falls.

explain: 뉴스에서는 '긴축 정책', '긴축 재정'처럼 나라나 회사가 돈 쓰는 것을 줄일 때 써요. 가정에서는 '긴축 모드'처럼 농담 섞어 말하기도 해요. 반대 방향의 말은 '확장'이에요.
explain_en: In the news it appears as '긴축 정책' or '긴축 재정' when a country or company cuts spending. At home people sometimes say '긴축 모드' jokingly. The opposite direction is '확장' (expansion).

examples.en: The company decided to tighten its budget this year.

examples.ko: 나라 살림을 긴축한 뒤에 복지가 줄었어요.
examples.en: After the nation tightened its finances, welfare shrank.
My pay went down, so I cut back on living expenses.
The government said it would tighten its finances.
Now is the time to tighten spending.

examples.ko: 너무 긴축하면 오히려 경기가 더 나빠질 수 있어요.
examples.en: If you tighten too much, the economy could actually get worse.

explain: 지출, 예산, 재정, 살림처럼 돈과 관련된 말을 목적어로 써요. 뉴스와 경제 이야기에서 주로 나오고, 개인이 아끼는 일은 보통 '아끼다', '허리띠를 졸라매다'라고 해요.
explain_en: Its objects are money-related words such as spending, budget, finances and household. It mostly appears in news and economic talk; for personal saving people usually say '아끼다' or '허리띠를 졸라매다'.

examples.en: I have something important to ask of you.
I have something important to tell you, teacher.

examples.ko: 친구가 긴히 상의할 게 있다고 전화했어요.
examples.en: A friend called to say he had something important to discuss.

examples.ko: 오늘 저녁에 긴히 의논할 일이 있는데 시간 돼요?
examples.en: I have something important to discuss tonight; do you have time?

examples.ko: 그분이 긴히 찾으신다고 하니 가 보세요.
examples.en: He says he urgently wants to see you, so please go.

examples.ko: 긴히 할 얘기가 있다고 해서 따로 만났어요.
examples.en: He said he had something serious to say, so we met privately.

explain: 부탁, 말씀, 상의, 의논 같은 말 앞에서 '중요하고 급한 일이 있다'는 느낌을 줘요. 조금 격식 있고 약간 옛스러운 말투라서 일상에서는 '급하게', '꼭'을 쓰기도 해요. 주로 '긴히 부탁할 게 있어요' 같은 표현으로 나와요.
explain_en: Before words like request, remark, consultation and discussion, it gives the feeling that something important and pressing is coming. It sounds a bit formal and slightly old-fashioned, so in daily talk people may use '급하게' or '꼭' instead. It mostly appears in phrases like '긴히 부탁할 게 있어요'.

examples.en: Grandmother is drawing water from the well.

examples.ko: 마을 사람들은 샘에서 물을 긷는 일로 하루를 시작했어요.
examples.en: The villagers began the day by drawing water from the spring.

examples.ko: 물을 긷지 않아도 집에서 수도를 틀면 돼요.
examples.en: You don't have to draw water; just turn on the tap at home.
The well is deep, so it's hard to draw water.

examples.ko: 양동이로 물을 긷고 나서 밥을 지었어요.
examples.en: After drawing water with a bucket, I cooked rice.

examples.ko: 아버지가 물을 긷던 우물이 아직 마을에 있어요.
examples.en: The well where my father used to draw water is still in the village.

explain: 우물이나 샘에서 물을 퍼 올릴 때 쓰는 말이라 요즘은 옛날이야기나 시골 이야기에서 더 많이 나와요. ㄷ 불규칙이라 '길어요, 길은, 길으면'으로 바뀌고 '긷고, 긷지, 긷는'은 그대로예요. 형용사 '길다'의 '길어요'와 모양이 같아서 문장 속 뜻으로 구별해요.
explain_en: It is used for drawing water from a well or spring, so today it appears more in old tales and stories of the countryside. It is a ㄷ-irregular verb: it changes to 길어요, 길은, 길으면, while 긷고, 긷지, 긷는 stay the same. '길어요' looks identical to that of the adjective '길다' (long), so tell them apart by context.

examples.en: My younger sibling got angry and jumped up and down in a rage.

examples.ko: 그 얘기를 듣고 아버지가 길길이 화를 내셨어요.
examples.en: Hearing that, my father flew into a rage.

examples.ko: 손님이 길길이 날뛰는 바람에 직원들이 놀랐어요.
examples.en: The staff were startled because the customer was raging wildly.

examples.ko: 억울하다고 길길이 소리를 지르던 사람이 누구예요?
examples.en: Who was the person shouting wildly that it was unfair?

examples.ko: 그렇게 길길이 뛴다고 상황이 바뀌지 않아요.
examples.en: Raging like that won't change the situation.
He leapt up in a fury, saying it wasn't true.

explain: 화가 나서 몹시 흥분해 날뛰는 모습을 말해요. 보통 '뛰다', '날뛰다'와 같이 쓰고, 기쁜 일에는 쓰지 않아요. 말투가 거칠고 생생해서 대화나 이야기에서 어울려요.
explain_en: It describes someone so angry and worked up that they thrash around. It usually goes with '뛰다' or '날뛰다' and is not used for happy things. The tone is vivid and rough, so it suits conversation and storytelling.

examples.ko: 저는 길눈이 밝아서 한 번 간 곳은 잊지 않아요.
examples.en: I have a good sense of direction, so I never forget a place I've been once.

examples.ko: 남편은 길눈이 어두워서 늘 내비게이션을 켜요.
examples.en: My husband has a poor sense of direction, so he always turns on the navigation.
A friend with a good sense of direction took the lead.
Is a sense of direction something you're born with, or can practice improve it?

examples.ko: 저는 길눈이 없어서 동네에서도 길을 잃어요.
examples.en: I have no sense of direction, so I get lost even in my own neighborhood.
Do people with a good sense of direction also drive well?

explain: 길을 잘 찾고 기억하는 능력이라서 '길눈이 밝다', '길눈이 어둡다'로 자주 말해요. 길을 잘 못 찾는 사람은 일상에서 '길치'라고도 해요. 한 번 간 길을 잘 기억할 때 칭찬하는 말로 쓸 수 있어요.
explain_en: It means the ability to find and remember routes, and it is commonly said as '길눈이 밝다' (good) or '길눈이 어둡다' (poor). In daily talk, someone who can't find their way is also called a '길치'. You can use it to praise someone who remembers routes well after one visit.

examples.ko: 이 책은 처음 한국어를 배우는 사람을 위한 길라잡이예요.
examples.en: This book is a guide for people learning Korean for the first time.
I planned the route after looking at a travel guide.

examples.ko: 선생님은 우리에게 인생의 길라잡이가 되어 주셨어요.
examples.en: Our teacher became a guide in life for us.
I received a guidebook for new employees.

examples.ko: 좋은 길라잡이 덕분에 산을 안전하게 올랐어요.
examples.en: Thanks to a good guide, we climbed the mountain safely.

examples.ko: 이 글을 작은 길라잡이로 삼아 보세요.
examples.en: Try using this text as a small guide.

explain: 길을 안내하는 사람뿐 아니라 입문서나 안내서, 어떤 일의 방향을 알려 주는 사람이나 글에도 써요. 책 제목에 '~ 길라잡이'가 자주 붙어요. 비슷한 말로 '길잡이', '안내자'가 있어요.
explain_en: It means not only a person who leads the way but also an introductory book, guidebook, or a person or text that shows the direction of something. '~ 길라잡이' often appears in book titles. Similar words are '길잡이' and '안내자'.

examples.en: I hope last night's dream was a lucky one.
People say a dream about a pig is a lucky dream.

examples.ko: 길몽을 꾼 날은 복권을 사 보고 싶어요.
examples.en: On a day when I've had a lucky dream, I want to try buying a lottery ticket.
Grandmother was happy from the morning, saying it was a lucky dream.

examples.ko: 시험 전날에 길몽 같은 꿈을 꿨어요.
examples.en: The day before the exam I had a dream that seemed like a lucky one.
I can't tell whether this is a good omen dream or a bad one.

explain: 좋은 일이 생길 징조로 여기는 꿈이에요. '길몽을 꾸다'처럼 말하고, 반대는 '흉몽'이에요. 어떤 꿈이 길몽인지는 사람마다 생각이 달라서, 평소에는 그냥 '좋은 꿈 꿨어요'라고도 해요.
explain_en: It is a dream regarded as a sign that something good will happen. You say '길몽을 꾸다', and the opposite is '흉몽'. Which dreams count as lucky differs from person to person, and in everyday talk people also just say '좋은 꿈 꿨어요'.

examples.en: We chose an auspicious day for the wedding date.
I looked on the calendar for a good auspicious day to move.

examples.ko: 어머니는 길일에 맞춰 개업 날짜를 정하셨어요.
examples.en: My mother set the opening day to match an auspicious day.
Today is an auspicious day, so there are lots of weddings.

examples.ko: 길일이든 아니든 우리 편한 날에 하자고요.
examples.en: Auspicious or not, let's do it on a day that suits us.
Of this year's auspicious days, how many fall on a weekend?

explain: 결혼, 이사, 개업 같은 큰일을 하기에 좋다고 여기는 날이에요. 이사 날짜를 말할 때 '손 없는 날'이라는 말도 같이 많이 써요. 반대로 나쁘다고 여기는 날은 '흉일'이라고 해요.
explain_en: It is a day considered good for big events such as weddings, moving and opening a business. When talking about moving dates, people also often say '손 없는 날'. A day considered bad is called '흉일'.

examples.en: They say that if a magpie cries in the morning, it's a good omen.

examples.ko: 새해 첫날에 무지개가 뜨면 길조 같아요.
examples.en: A rainbow on New Year's Day seems like a good omen.

examples.ko: 이번 합격 소식은 좋은 일의 길조 같아요.
examples.en: This news of passing feels like a sign of good things to come.

examples.ko: 길조가 보이니까 오늘 일이 잘될 것 같아요.
examples.en: I see a good sign, so today's work will probably go well.

examples.ko: 저는 길조도 흉조도 별로 믿지 않아요.
examples.en: I don't really believe in good omens or bad omens.
That bird is regarded as a good omen in the village.

explain: 좋은 일이 생길 것 같은 조짐을 말해요. 한국에서는 까치가 울면 반가운 소식이 온다고 해서 까치를 길조로 여겨요. 반대는 '흉조'이고, 일상에서는 '좋은 징조'라고도 말해요.
explain_en: It means a sign that something good is likely to happen. In Korea the magpie is seen as a lucky bird, since its cry is said to bring welcome news. The opposite is '흉조', and in daily speech people also say '좋은 징조'.

examples.ko: 새 한 쌍이 처마 밑에 깃들였어요.
examples.en: A pair of birds nested under the eaves.

examples.ko: 이 노래에는 어머니의 사랑이 깃들여 있어요.
examples.en: A mother's love dwells in this song.
I observed the animals that make their home in the old forest.

examples.ko: 선물에 정성이 깃들인 것 같아서 고마웠어요.
examples.en: I was thankful because the gift seemed full of sincere care.

examples.ko: 작은 집에 가족의 추억이 깃들이기 시작했어요.
examples.en: Family memories began to settle into the small house.

examples.ko: 이 그림에는 작가의 슬픔이 깃들이어 있는 것 같아요.
examples.en: The artist's sorrow seems to dwell in this painting.

explain: 새가 둥지를 틀고 사는 것에서, 정성, 추억, 역사, 감정이 어떤 곳에 스며 있다는 뜻으로도 써요. 주로 글이나 설명에서 쓰고, 일상 대화에서는 '담겨 있다'를 더 많이 말해요. 비슷한 말로 '깃들다'도 있어요.
explain_en: Starting from birds nesting somewhere, it is also used when care, memories, history or feelings are present in a place or thing. It is mostly used in writing and explanations; in everyday talk people more often say '담겨 있다'. A similar word is '깃들다'.

examples.en: My son shaved his head and now has a buzz cut.

examples.ko: 옛날 사진 속 아버지는 까까머리 중학생이었어요.
examples.en: In the old photo, my father was a buzz-cut middle schooler.
I met friends from my buzz-cut days after a long time.

examples.ko: 군대에 가기 전에 까까머리로 자르고 왔어요.
examples.en: Before going into the army, he came back with a buzz cut.
Because I have a buzz cut, I always wear a hat in winter.
I touched my younger brother's buzz cut, and it felt bristly.

explain: 머리카락을 아주 짧게 깎은 머리를 말하는데, 옛날 남학생의 머리를 떠올리게 하고 친근하거나 귀여운 느낌이 있어요. 요즘 일상에서는 '삭발'이나 '스포츠머리'라고도 해요. 다만 '삭발'은 머리를 완전히 미는 것에 더 가까워요.
explain_en: It means hair cut very short, and it brings to mind schoolboys of the past, with a friendly or cute feel. In daily speech people today also say '삭발' or '스포츠머리'. However, '삭발' is closer to shaving the head completely.
